main_stories.title: World Leaders Navigate Complex Diplomatic Tensions Amid Trade, Security Disputes
main_stories.narrative: OTTAWA, Canada — Global leaders faced mounting diplomatic pressures this week as Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney rejected U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's claims that he walked back critical comments about American trade policy, while Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum suspended oil shipments to Cuba amid pressure from President Donald Trump. British Prime Minister Keir Starmer secured trade agreements with China during his visit to Beijing, including reduced tariffs on Scotch whisky, even as Trump called UK-China business dealings "very dangerous," according to government officials. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy rejected Russia's invitation for peace talks in Moscow and instead invited Russian President Vladimir Putin to Kyiv, while Chinese President Xi Jinping told Putin during a video call that their nations need a "grand plan" to develop ties. The diplomatic maneuvering comes as NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte dismissed calls for a separate European army and warned that Europe cannot defend itself without U.S. military support.

main_stories.title: Starmer says Andrew should testify to US Congress on Epstein
main_stories.narrative: TOKYO, Japan — British Prime Minister Keir Starmer said Saturday that Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor should testify before the U.S. Congress about his ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, following the release of new Justice Department files containing photographs and emails. "Anybody who has got information should be prepared to share that information in whatever form they are asked to do that," Starmer told reporters on his plane to Japan. "You can't be victim centred if you're not prepared to do that." The files released Friday included images appearing to show the former prince kneeling over an unidentified woman and emails showing he maintained contact with Epstein after the financier's 2008 conviction for soliciting paid sex from a minor. Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, who was stripped of his royal titles in October, has repeatedly denied wrongdoing in connection with Epstein.

main_stories.title: Columnist warns Labour electoral stance could enable Reform victory
main_stories.narrative: LONDON, Britain — Guardian columnist George Monbiot warned that Prime Minister Keir Starmer's refusal to reform Britain's electoral system could enable the far-right Reform UK party to take power with a minority of votes. Monbiot said Labour's insistence on maintaining the first-past-the-post voting system, despite party conference support for proportional representation, stems from self-interest rather than principle. He cited analysis suggesting Reform UK could win 48% of parliamentary seats with just 27% of the vote under the current system. Monbiot said Starmer previously criticized the electoral system as unfair while seeking party leadership but abandoned reform efforts after taking office. The columnist argued that under proportional representation, Labour would face near elimination based on current Welsh polling data, explaining the party's resistance to change.

main_stories.title: German Chancellor Merz prioritizes economy as unemployment hits 12-year high
main_stories.narrative: BERLIN, Germany — German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Friday that boosting the economy would be his main focus this year after unemployment surged past 3 million to a 12-year high. Labor Office data showed 177,000 more people out of work in January than December, bringing the total to 3.08 million and pushing the unemployment rate to 6.6%. "The rise in the number of unemployed to more than three million is an alarm signal," Merz wrote on social media platform X. The jobless figures highlighted the lag from economic stagnation despite fourth-quarter GDP growth of 0.3%, which beat forecasts. Economy Minister Katherina Reiche said Germany must pivot toward new "growth engines," arguing that traditional export strengths "no longer carry our growth."

main_stories.title: German chancellor calls Europe alternative to imperialism, autocracy
main_stories.narrative: BERLIN, Germany — German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Thursday that the European Union represents an "alternative to imperialism and autocracy" as great power rivalries intensify globally. Speaking to parliament about foreign policy, Merz said Europe can forge partnerships with democracies based on "mutual respect, trust and reliability" in an increasingly competitive world. He emphasized that while Germany seeks continued cooperation with the United States, it will not act as a "subordinate" in the relationship. Merz also defended Germany's military deployment in Afghanistan after U.S. President Donald Trump suggested non-American NATO troops avoided front-line combat, noting that 59 German soldiers died during the nearly 20-year mission.

main_stories.title: UK's Starmer arrives in China, first PM visit since 2018
main_stories.narrative: BEIJING, China — British Prime Minister Keir Starmer arrived in China on Wednesday for the first visit by a UK leader since 2018, encouraging businesses to seize opportunities while acknowledging security concerns. "Eight years since a British prime minister stepped on Chinese soil. So on this delegation you're making history," Starmer told more than 50 business leaders accompanying him, according to Reuters. The prime minister said he hoped to make "progress" on visa-free travel between the countries and insisted Britain could strengthen economic ties with China without angering the United States. Starmer is scheduled to meet President Xi Jinping and Premier Li Qiang on Thursday as part of efforts to mend UK-China relations after years of tensions over Hong Kong, China's support for Russia, and espionage allegations.

main_stories.title: Starmer defends China engagement after Trump criticism
main_stories.narrative: SHANGHAI, China — Prime Minister Keir Starmer said Friday it would be "foolhardy" for Britain to ignore China, rejecting President Donald Trump's assertion that closer UK-China ties are "very dangerous." Starmer's comments to the BBC came after three hours of talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping that resulted in China agreeing to cut tariffs on UK whisky and relax visa rules. Trump, responding to questions about the closer UK-China relationship, said "it's very dangerous for them to do that" but did not elaborate. Starmer said the UK-U.S. relationship remains "very close" and that Washington had been made aware of his visit, adding that "for the UK to be the only country that refuses to engage would not be in our national interest."

international_stories.title: Starmer defends China visit after Trump warning
international_stories.narrative: SHANGHAI, China — British Prime Minister Keir Starmer said Friday that the U.K. "can't stick its head in the sand" regarding China, defending his trade mission after U.S. President Donald Trump warned against deals between Beijing and London. Starmer, who arrived in Shanghai with more than 50 business leaders, told Sky News that Trump's criticism was aimed more at Canada than Britain and noted that Washington was aware of his trip in advance. "China is the second biggest economy in the world. Along with Hong Kong, it's our third-biggest trading partner. And through this visit, we've opened up lots of opportunities for jobs and wealth creation," Starmer said. Trump had called it "very dangerous" for Britain to pursue deals with China, though he said it was "even more dangerous" for Canada to engage with Beijing.

international_stories.title: Sheinbaum recalls US military attacks, defends Mexican sovereignty
international_stories.narrative: BAVISPE, Mexico — President Claudia Sheinbaum recalled historical U.S. military attacks against Mexico and said she continues fighting for national sovereignty during a visit Friday to this border town 100 kilometers from the United States. Speaking in Sonora state, Sheinbaum referenced past military interventions by the U.S. while asserting Mexico's ongoing struggle for sovereignty, according to Mexican media reports. The remarks came as Sheinbaum visited the northern border region, where U.S.-Mexico relations remain a key concern.

international_stories.title: Macron's 'for sure' comment at Davos goes viral
international_stories.narrative: DAVOS, Switzerland — French President Emmanuel Macron's heavily accented pronunciation of "for sure" during a World Economic Forum speech has sparked thousands of online parodies and remixes, according to French media reports. Macron said Europe "sometimes is too slow, for sure" on Tuesday, emphasizing the final two words with what Le Monde described as an "exaggerated" accent. The French Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs' satirical social media account posted "Fo shur" in response to the viral moment, Le Monde reported. The incident has generated T-shirts, electronic music remixes and widespread social media commentary across multiple countries.

entities.name: Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs

international_stories.title: Finland's Stubb criticizes Trump's foreign policy ideology
international_stories.narrative: HELSINKI, Finland — President Alexander Stubb criticized the United States' foreign policy under Donald Trump during his opening address to parliament, saying the current administration's ideology contradicts Finnish values by undermining the international system. Stubb said Europe can no longer rely on the United States and described what he called "ruthless opportunism" by major powers as short-sighted, according to Helsingin Sanomat. The Finnish president outlined how Finland should navigate the changing global order, stating the country must choose whether to be a diplomatic player or a pawn and should "choose its battles" while always defending state sovereignty and territorial integrity. Stubb said Finland would cooperate with the U.S. on defense, NATO and maritime industry issues but would openly disagree on climate change and international organizations.

international_stories.title: Finland's Stubb says US ties remain strong despite ideological differences
international_stories.narrative: HELSINKI, Finland — Finnish President Alexander Stubb said Wednesday that bilateral cooperation between Finland and the United States will remain strong despite what he called ideological differences with the current U.S. administration. Speaking at the ceremonial opening of Finland's 2026 parliamentary session, Stubb said the current U.S. administration is guided by what he described as MAGA and America First ideologies that are foreign to Finns. "[MAGA] diminishes the international, rules-based world order and, for example, the European Union. We disagree with the United States on this ideology," Stubb said. The Finnish president said he remains confident in continued U.S.-Finland cooperation because Finland's defense capabilities and Arctic security serve American interests, particularly as Finland operates on NATO's front line.

international_stories.title: Finnish president criticizes US foreign policy ideology at parliament opening
international_stories.narrative: HELSINKI, Finland — President Alexander Stubb said the current U.S. administration's foreign policy is based on an ideology that conflicts with Finnish and European values by undermining the international system, speaking at the opening of parliament without naming President Donald Trump. Stubb said the U.S. operates more outside international institutions and has relegated Europe behind the Western Hemisphere and Asia-Pacific region in its priorities. The Finnish president said the bilateral relationship between Finland and the U.S. remains strong enough to allow direct discussion of disagreements on issues like climate change and international institutions. Stubb cited recent tensions over Greenland as an example of changes in U.S. foreign policy approach, stating that Finland must continue making choices as it adapts to this new reality.

domestic_stories.title: Mexico's Sheinbaum confirms electoral reform agreement with allies
domestic_stories.narrative: MEXICO CITY, Mexico — President Claudia Sheinbaum confirmed Tuesday that her government has reached an agreement with allied parties to advance electoral reform legislation that will be sent to Congress in February. Sheinbaum said the reform is underway and its submission is imminent, stating "my objective is to have it for next week, but what is certain is that it is in February." The president said the reform will strengthen oversight of money allocated to parties and campaigns, including measures to prevent organized crime financing. However, Senate coordinator Manuel Velasco Coello of the Green Party said no agreement exists yet, stating his party disagrees with some proposals, particularly changes to proportional representation that could affect democratic balance.

domestic_stories.title: Mexico president inaugurates final section of Mexico City-Toluca train
domestic_stories.narrative: MEXICO CITY, Mexico — President Claudia Sheinbaum on Monday inaugurated the final section of the Mexico City-Toluca Interurban Train, completing a major transportation project linking the capital with Mexico State. The president opened the Santa Fe and Observatorio stations, the last two needed to complete the route, according to Mexican media reports. Sheinbaum said the construction faced significant technical and environmental challenges, including building a cable-stayed bridge over an active spring to avoid environmental damage. Jorge Mendoza Sanchez, director of the National Bank of Public Works and Services, said tickets for the full route from Observatorio to Toluca will cost 90 pesos ($4.50), with varying fares depending on distance traveled.

domestic_stories.title: Mexico's Sheinbaum inaugurates long-delayed Insurgente train line
domestic_stories.narrative: MEXICO CITY, Mexico — President Claudia Sheinbaum on Monday inaugurated the Insurgente train line connecting Mexico City to the Toluca metropolitan area, completing a project that took 12 years and required a multimillion-dollar investment, according to La Jornada newspaper. Sheinbaum cut the inaugural ribbon alongside Mexico City Mayor Clara Brugada and Mexico State Governor Delfina Gómez before taking the first official ride on the final two stations that opened to the public. The train line, which began construction in 2014 under former President Enrique Peña Nieto's administration, connects the Toluca suburbs to Mexico City's Observatorio Metro station. Public service began at 4 p.m., with hundreds of people waiting outside Observatorio station and chanting "Viva Mexico!" when doors opened, the newspaper reported.

domestic_stories.title: Polish President Calls Security Council Meeting on Parliament Speaker
domestic_stories.narrative: WARSAW, Poland — President Karol Nawrocki called a National Security Council meeting for Feb. 11 to examine alleged business contacts between Parliament Speaker Włodzimierz Czarzasty's wife and a Russian citizen, presidential spokesman Rafał Leśkiewicz said Tuesday. Deputy Parliament Speaker Piotr Zgorzelski criticized the agenda as "embarrassing" and urged Nawrocki to remove the item, calling it "disproportionate" to media reports about Czarzasty's wife's art market dealings with a Russian national allegedly linked to Russian state-controlled financial institutions. The Parliament Chancellery said Czarzasty receives full counterintelligence protection and access to classified information, adding that security services would have acted if any threat existed. Czarzasty has rejected the allegations, saying no formal charges or investigations exist and the matter is purely political.

domestic_stories.title: Polish President Nawrocki seeks expanded political control, analyst says
domestic_stories.narrative: WARSAW, Poland — President Karol Nawrocki is pursuing a strategy to consolidate political dominance by blocking key appointments and demanding meetings with security chiefs and parliamentary leaders, according to political analyst Michał Szułdrzyński. Szułdrzyński said Nawrocki blocked nominations for intelligence graduates and diplomatic posts while insisting on meetings with intelligence service heads, despite Prime Minister Donald Tusk's initial resistance. The Civic Coalition and Left parties refused invitations to meet with Nawrocki at the Presidential Palace, with Szułdrzyński stating they "deciphered the president's game" and chose not to participate in what he called a "staged spectacle." Szułdrzyński said the president's actions aim to show "who is the boss of all bosses" rather than seeking genuine cooperation with the ruling coalition.

domestic_stories.title: Polish President Nawrocki pardons three convicted individuals
domestic_stories.narrative: WARSAW, Poland — President Karol Nawrocki pardoned three convicted individuals while rejecting five other clemency requests, the Presidential Chancellery said in a statement. Nawrocki reviewed eight clemency applications submitted by Prosecutor General Waldemar Żurek, according to the chancellery. The pardoned individuals included a person convicted of causing a fatal traffic accident, another convicted of economic crimes, and a third convicted of criminal threats, the statement said. The president cited humanitarian reasons, including poor health conditions and advanced age of the convicted persons, as primary factors in his decisions, according to the chancellery.

domestic_stories.title: Polish President Nawrocki leads trust poll, survey shows
domestic_stories.narrative: WARSAW, Poland — Polish President Karol Nawrocki topped a new trust ranking with 52% approval, followed by Deputy Prime Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz at 46% and Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski at 45%, according to a CBOS poll released this week. The survey, conducted Jan. 8-20 among 938 adult Polish residents, showed Warsaw Mayor Rafał Trzaskowski at 42% trust and Prime Minister Donald Tusk at 41%. Former Prime Minister Jarosław Kaczyński, leader of the opposition Law and Justice party, ranked 15th with 26% trust and 56% distrust, the polling center said.

domestic_stories.title: Finnish President Stubb visits Vantaa, calls city 'really nice'
domestic_stories.narrative: VANTAA, Finland — President Alexander Stubb visited the city of Vantaa on Tuesday, calling it a 'really nice' city during his first official visit there with his wife Suzanne Innes-Stubb. The visit culminated at the Jumbo shopping center, where dozens of residents lined up for photos with the presidential couple, according to Helsingin Sanomat. Stubb said Vantaa represents bicycle shops, triathlon competitions and children's floorball activities to him, and told residents to 'be Vantaalans.' Earlier in the day, the presidential couple visited Hakunila's Lehtikuusi school and the Finnish Red Cross Blood Service headquarters.
